opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Daniel. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential and won't be linked to your name.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Absolutely. This is my favourite topic, so stop me if I get carried away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I say to every principal: used well, these tools give teachers back hours every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's roughly what my pilots show. Teachers save time on planning and marking. If it stays a tool, I keep running pilots and it's a good, steady job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Expand the pilots to a few more schools. Write proper guidance for teachers on what to use and what to avoid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Energised.

S0.say: Used well, these tools give teachers back hours every week.
S0.think: His pilots show time saved on planning and marking. If it stays a tool, he has a good, steady job.
S0.do: Expands the pilots and writes clear guidance for teachers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is our window to do it right in schools, before the pressure arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slow is the best case for my work. Time to test things, find what actually helps kids, and drop what doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Set up a proper study with a university partner across the district. Train a group of lead teachers in each school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, honestly.

S1.say: This is our window to do it right in schools, before the pressure arrives.
S1.think: Slow change is his best case, with time to test what really helps children.
S1.do: Sets up a district-wide study with a university and trains lead teachers in each school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say students need to learn to work alongside AI, and our district is ready because we started early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the evidence is more mixed than you say in public. Why not say so?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because funding follows confidence. If I sound unsure, the pilots get cut and we lose the chance to learn. It's a balance I'm not proud of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job gets bigger, not smaller. Everyone suddenly wants an AI plan. Between us, the evidence on learning is more mixed than I let on in public. Saving teachers time is clear. Better results for kids, less so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask for a bigger team and budget while there's political will. Be more honest in my reports about what isn't working, because a big rollout on weak evidence would come back on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, with a small nag about the evidence.

S2.say: Students need to learn to work alongside AI, and our district is ready because we started early.
S2.think: His job grows, but the evidence on learning is more mixed than he says in public.
S2.do: Asks for more team and budget, and reports more honestly on what isn't working.
S2.feel: Excited, with a small nag about the evidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say schools have to change what they teach, fast. Less memorising, more judgement, more working with people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI matches professionals, someone on the school board will ask why we need a human edtech lead when a vendor's AI can plan the rollout. And with a political crisis, budgets swing wildly. My job is safer than most, but it isn't safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Make myself the person who knows the teachers and the families, not just the software. Put the share gains towards paying off debt. Keep a list of vendor jobs I could move to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Less sure of my footing.

S3.say: Schools have to change what they teach fast, towards judgement and working with people.
S3.think: A vendor's AI could plan the rollout, and budgets would swing in the crisis. His job is safer than most, but not safe.
S3.do: Makes himself the person who knows teachers and families, pays down debt with share gains and lists vendor jobs he could move to.
S3.feel: Uneasy, less sure of his footing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say schools are now the most important public service we have, because they're where people learn what to do next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots don't change much for me. If anything, a society that needs to retrain everyone needs people like me to run it. I'd probably come out of this okay. My worry is for families in the district who won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said your job wasn't safe. Now you say you'd come out okay. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I think. My current title might go. But someone who can help a whole community learn new tools will be needed. I'm betting on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pitch the district on running evening retraining for parents in our school buildings. That's a real use for what I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady. A bit uneasy for others.

S4.say: Schools are now the most important public service, because they're where people learn what to do next.
S4.think: A society retraining everyone needs people like him. His title might go, but he'd probably come out okay.
S4.do: Pitches evening retraining for parents in school buildings.
S4.feel: Mostly steady, a bit uneasy for others.
